question.problem:
$$ \{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=2y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-2x(t)+1,\end{aligned}\,[\begin{aligned}x(0) \\ y(0)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] $$ Find the solution to the initial value problem above. *Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}].$*
$[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{2}\,\,$ {{field-1}}
$3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)$
question.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t)+g(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and $g(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}]\text{d}s \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}]}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$
